summary: Defines an optional, transitive BGP attribute for announcing BGP Prefix Segment Identifiers, which are used by Segment Routing. It also specifies how receiving routers process it, so Segment Routing can be used where BGP carries the labels.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 8669 lets a BGP advertisement say which numbered instruction belongs to a destination prefix. A router that receives it adds that number to the range of labels it has set aside for itself, and programs the result. That is what lets a path be built out of instructions when the prefixes come from BGP rather than from an IGP.

questions: what is the bgp prefix-sid attribute
what is a label index in segment routing
subtitle: A BGP attribute that hands out a numbered label index for each prefix, so Segment Routing can run over BGP in MPLS networks.

tldr.problem: Segment Routing normally learns about a prefix's identifier from an IGP, but many networks carry their prefixes in BGP, and a controller needs to know the identifier that goes with a BGP prefix.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines an optional transitive BGP path attribute, type code 40, that carries a Label-Index TLV with the index a router assigned to a prefix. Each router combines that index with its own Segment Routing Global Block to derive the label it installs.
tldr.outcome: BGP can now carry the same kind of segment identifier an IGP would, and a router that finds the derived label falls outside its own range, or two prefixes claiming the same index, discards the attribute and falls back to ordinary labelled unicast behaviour.

facts.label: SRGB range encoding
facts.value: 3 octets for the first label, 3 for the count

today: RFC 8669 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted. It registers the BGP Prefix-SID path attribute with the type code 40, the BGP Prefix-SID TLV Types registry, and two empty flags registries for the Label-Index and Originator SRGB TLVs.

sections.title: What a BGP Prefix-SID Is
sections.content:
When Segment Routing is applied to the MPLS data plane, the segment identifier consists of a label. Segment Routing can also be applied to an IPv6 data plane, using an IPv6 routing header containing a stack of segment identifiers encoded as IPv6 addresses, but the applicability of Segment Routing over IPv6 is beyond the scope of this document.

A BGP Prefix Segment is a BGP prefix with a Prefix-SID attached. A BGP Prefix-SID is always a global segment identifier within the Segment Routing domain, and it identifies an instruction to forward the packet over the Equal-Cost Multipath best path computed by BGP to the related prefix. The BGP Prefix-SID is the identifier of the BGP Prefix Segment, and the document always refers to the segment by that identifier.

This document defines the BGP extensions that signal the BGP Prefix-SID: a BGP attribute known as the BGP Prefix-SID attribute, and the rules to originate, receive and handle error conditions for it. The attribute can be attached to prefixes from Multiprotocol BGP IPv4 and IPv6 Labeled Unicast. Its use with other address family combinations is not defined here.

Two points are worth noting. A BGP Prefix-SID will be global across autonomous systems when the interconnected systems are part of the same Segment Routing domain; otherwise the border routers of each domain have to handle the advertisement of unique identifiers, and the mechanisms for that interconnection are outside the scope of the document. And a BGP Prefix-SID may be attached to a BGP prefix, which implies each prefix is advertised individually, reducing the ability to pack BGP advertisements with shared attributes.
sections.plainLanguage: A segment identifier tells the network what instruction to apply to a packet. In an MPLS network that instruction is a label. This RFC attaches such an identifier to a prefix carried in BGP, so that networks whose prefixes live in BGP can also build paths out of instructions.

sections.title: From a Label Index to a Label
sections.content:
The operator assigns a globally unique label index to a locally originated prefix of a BGP speaker, and advertises it to the other BGP speakers in the Segment Routing domain. Each BGP speaker is configured with a label block called the Segment Routing Global Block. While the Segment Routing architecture recommends using the same block across all nodes in the domain, the block of a node is a local property and could differ between speakers.

If traffic engineering within the domain is required, each node may also have to advertise topological information and Peer SIDs for its links and peers, which is done through the BGP Link State extensions.

Where a prefix segment is to be included in an MPLS label stack, for example for traffic engineering, the originator's block is needed in order to compute the local label used by the originator. The document assumes that BGP-LS is the preferred method for collecting peer segments and block information, but as an optional alternative for advertising the local block alone, without topology and without applicability to traffic engineering, it defines the Originator SRGB TLV.

A BGP speaker derives its local MPLS label L from the label index L_I and its local block, and then programs that label in its MPLS data plane as the incoming, or local, label for the prefix. The outgoing label is found in the NLRI of the Multiprotocol BGP IPv4 or IPv6 Labeled Unicast prefix advertisement; the label index is only used as a hint to derive the local label.
sections.plainLanguage: Each router keeps a private range of labels, its block. The number that travels in BGP is an offset into that range, not a label in itself, so the same number can be used by different routers for different things. A receiving router adds the offset to the start of its own block and programs the result as the label for that prefix.

sections.title: The Attribute and Its Two TLVs
sections.content:
The BGP Prefix-SID attribute is an optional, transitive BGP path attribute with the type code 40 assigned by IANA. It is defined as a set of elements encoded as Type, Length, Value tuples. Every TLV starts with a 1-octet type and a 2-octet length. Two TLVs are defined: the Label-Index TLV and the Originator SRGB TLV, both used only when Segment Routing is applied to the MPLS data plane. For future extensibility, unknown TLVs must be ignored and propagated unmodified.

The Label-Index TLV must be present in the attribute attached to IPv4 or IPv6 Labeled Unicast prefixes, and must be ignored when received for other address family combinations. It has a type of 1 and a length of 7 octets. The value holds an 8-bit reserved field, which must be clear on transmission and ignored on reception; a 16-bit flags field, none of which are defined by this document and which must also be clear on transmission and ignored on reception; and a 32-bit label index, the index value in the block space.

The Originator SRGB TLV is optional, with a type of 3. Its length is 2 plus a non-zero multiple of 6 octets. It holds a 16-bit flags field, clear on transmission and ignored on reception, and then one or more ranges, each made of 3 octets giving the first label in the range and 3 octets giving the number of labels in it. The field may appear several times, in which case the block consists of the concatenated ranges.

The Originator SRGB TLV carries the block of the node that originated the prefix, and it must not be changed during the propagation of the update. It is used to build SR policies where different blocks are in use. It may only appear on IPv4 or IPv6 Labeled Unicast prefixes, and is ignored elsewhere.

IANA has created the BGP Prefix-SID TLV Types registry: 0 and 255 are reserved, 1 is Label-Index, 2 is deprecated, 3 is Originator SRGB, and 4 to 254 are unassigned, with Expert Review for new values. The value 2 previously corresponded to the IPv6 SID TLV in earlier versions of the document; it was removed and use of the attribute for Segment Routing over IPv6 is deferred to future specifications. Two empty 16-bit flags registries were also created, one for the Label-Index TLV and one for the Originator SRGB TLV.
sections.plainLanguage: The attribute is a small container holding two optional pieces of information: the offset for the prefix, which is mandatory, and the block the originator used, which is optional. Both are written as tagged blocks so that future versions can add more without breaking older readers.

sections.title: Receiving the Attribute
sections.content:
A BGP speaker receiving the attribute from an EBGP neighbour outside the boundaries of the Segment Routing domain must discard it unless it is configured to accept it from that neighbour, and should log an error when discarding it.

A session supporting the Multiprotocol BGP Labeled IPv4 or IPv6 Unicast address family is required. When the attribute is attached to such a prefix it must contain the Label-Index TLV and may contain the Originator SRGB TLV; an attribute received without a Label-Index TLV must be considered invalid.

The label index gives the receiving speaker guidance about the incoming label to allocate for the prefix. Given a label index L_I, the derived label is L_I plus SRGB_Start. The attribute is conflicting for a speaker M when the derived label lies outside the block configured on M, and otherwise acceptable. If several different prefixes are received with the same label index, all of them must be considered conflicting.

If several valid paths for the same prefix are received from multiple speakers, or from the same speaker where multiple paths are advertised, and the attributes do not contain the same label index, then the label index from the best path should be chosen, with the exception of route dampening. When a speaker receives a path with an acceptable attribute and selects it as the best path, it should program the derived label as the label for the prefix in its local MPLS data plane.

When a speaker receives a path with an invalid or conflicting attribute, or one it cannot process, it must ignore the attribute and assign a local, dynamic label that is not in the block, as in ordinary labelled unicast operation. An invalid attribute must follow the error handling rules, and an error should be logged. A conflicting attribute should not be treated as an error and should be propagated unchanged, with a warning logged for analysis. When an attribute changes from conflicting to acceptable, other prefixes may also become acceptable, and implementations should ensure that the affected prefixes revert to the newly acceptable label indices.
sections.plainLanguage: On receipt, the receiver checks the offset against its own range. If the resulting label is inside the range, the receiver installs it. If it falls outside, or if two prefixes claim the same offset, the receiver treats the attribute as unusable and falls back to a local label of its own choosing. The attribute is not an error, it simply cannot be trusted for that prefix.

sections.title: Advertising the Attribute
sections.content:
The attribute may be attached to BGP IPv4 or IPv6 Labeled Unicast prefixes. To prevent distribution of the attribute beyond its intended scope, attribute filtering should be deployed to remove it at the administrative boundary of the Segment Routing domain.

A speaker that advertises a path received from one of its neighbours should advertise the BGP Prefix-SID it received with that path, without modification, as long as the attribute was acceptable. If the path did not come with an attribute, the speaker may attach one if it is configured to do so, and the content of the TLVs is then determined by configuration.

A speaker that originates a prefix attaches the attribute when it advertises the prefix to its neighbours via Multiprotocol BGP IPv4 or IPv6 Labeled Unicast, and the value of the label index is determined by configuration. It may optionally announce the Originator SRGB TLV along with the mandatory Label-Index TLV.

Since the label index must be unique within the Segment Routing domain, by default an implementation should not advertise the attribute outside an autonomous system unless it is explicitly configured to do so. In all cases the label field of the advertised NLRI must be set to the local or incoming label programmed in the MPLS data plane for the prefix. If the prefix is associated with one of the speaker's interfaces, this is the usual MPLS label, such as the Implicit or Explicit NULL label.
sections.plainLanguage: A router that originates a prefix decides which offset to use and puts it in the advertisement. A router that passes the advertisement on passes the attribute through unchanged, as long as it found it usable. By default the attribute stops at the edge of the operator's own network, so the numbering scheme inside is not leaked to other networks.

sections.title: Error Handling
sections.content:
When a speaker receives an UPDATE containing a malformed or invalid BGP Prefix-SID attribute attached to an IPv4 or IPv6 Labeled Unicast prefix, it must ignore the attribute and not advertise it to other peers. A malformed attribute is one that cannot be parsed because it does not meet the minimum attribute length requirement, contains a TLV length that does not conform to the length constraints for the TLV, or contains a TLV length that would extend beyond the end of the attribute. This is equivalent to the attribute discard action of RFC 7606, and an error should be logged when an attribute is discarded.

As in RFC 7606, if the attribute appears more than once in an UPDATE message, all occurrences other than the first are discarded and the message continues to be processed. The same applies when a recognised TLV appears more than once inside the attribute but the specification allows only one occurrence: the later occurrences are discarded and the attribute continues to be processed. Unknown TLVs must be ignored and propagated unmodified.
sections.plainLanguage: If the attribute cannot be parsed, the receiver drops it and says so in its log, but it still processes the rest of the route update. The same is true of a repeated copy of the attribute or of a repeated copy of one of its parts: the first copy is used and the rest are dropped.

sections.title: Manageability Considerations
sections.content:
The document assumes that advertisement of the attribute is controlled by the operator, for two reasons. First, to prevent undesired origination and advertisement: by default the attribute should not be attached to a prefix and advertised, so advertisement should require explicit enablement. Second, to prevent undesired propagation: by default the attribute is not advertised outside the boundary of a single Segment Routing or administrative domain, which may include one or more autonomous systems, and propagation to other autonomous systems must be explicitly configured.

The deployment model described in RFC 8670 assumes multiple autonomous systems under a common administrative domain. For that use case the advertisement is applicable in the inter-AS context, that is to EBGP, while it stays confined to a single administrative domain.
sections.plainLanguage: Both the decision to publish the attribute at all and the decision to let it cross the edge of your own network belong to the operator. The defaults are off, so nothing changes until someone turns it on deliberately.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The attribute inherits the security considerations of RFC 4271, RFC 8277 and RFC 8402.

When advertised using BGPsec, as described in RFC 8205, the attribute imposes no unique security considerations, but it is not protected by the BGPsec signatures.

The deployment model assumes all nodes are under a single administrative domain, and it assumes the operator does not want to leak information about internal prefixes and topology outside that domain. The BGP Prefix-SID is part of that internal information, so the common BGP filtering mechanisms are applied at the boundary of the domain. Local attribute filtering policies are not standardized and are beyond the scope of the document.

To prevent a denial-of-service attack caused by excessive BGP updates carrying an invalid or conflicting attribute, rate limiting of error log messages and suppression of duplicate error messages should be deployed. Since BGP-LS is the preferred method for advertising block information, a speaker should log an error if it receives an attribute with block information different from the block it received for the same node in BGP-LS.
sections.plainLanguage: The attribute says something about the inside of your network, so it is filtered at the boundary by default. It is not covered by BGPsec signatures, which means a signed route can still carry an attribute that was tampered with, so the checks in the receiving rules matter.

items.title: Origination
items.text: By default no prefix carries the attribute; enabling it is an explicit choice.

items.title: Propagation
items.text: The attribute stops at the boundary of the administrative domain unless it is configured otherwise.

items.title: Filtering
items.text: Attribute filtering at the boundary keeps the internal numbering scheme private.
